title: Just set up my first profitable bot (in backtest , 29% CAGR )
author: mates__777
selftext:
Hi i am pretty new in this and i was researching a lot and i stumbled across some recommendation that the more simple the better and i used it found something ,  it worked great in backtesting , beat the market , tested for overfitting  and other , all have seem to pass ( i use Claude and data i pay for ) and i have it plugged in a demo account .   
And would like to ask if you have some recommendations , to maybe use other programs for backtesting or getting data from and what to watch out for

replies.author: mates__777
replies.body: I just use Claude code to backtest

comments.author: ryank001
comments.body:
nice work getting a full loop running — "keep it simple" is genuinely the right instinct, most people over-engineer and curve-fit themselves into a corner.

that said, gentle reality check on the 29% CAGR: that number's high enough that i'd assume it's flattered by something until proven otherwise. couple things i'd check before you trust it —

* **how many trades and over how long?** 29% over a couple years / a few dozen trades tells you almost nothing. i want 100+ trades across a full market cycle before i believe a curve.
* **did it live through a real crash?** if your backtest window is basically the post-2023 bull run, of course it looks great. drag it back through 2022, covid, 2008 if your data goes that far. a lot of "beat the market" bots quietly buy every step down into a crash and blow up.
* **break P&L down per-symbol.** i've had bots look +EV until i noticed one lucky ticker carried the entire profit and everything else was a wash.
* **watch the survivorship bias in your data** — if your universe is today's stocks/coins, the ones that died already got deleted, which inflates everything.

on tools: for stocks, backtrader or vectorbt (python) are solid and free; QuantConnect if you want built-in clean-ish data. for data, Polygon or Norgate (Norgate specifically includes delisted names, which kills survivorship bias — worth it). and yeah Claude/ChatGPT are great for *writing* the backtest, just don't let it grade its own homework — the "tested for overfitting, all passed" part is exactly where an LLM will cheerfully tell you what you want to hear.

biggest thing to watch out for: the demo account is where you find out if it's real. let it run forward on unseen data for a while before you even think about real money — forward results always come in worse than backtest, and how *much* worse tells you how overfit you were.

replies.author: mates__777
replies.body: Thanks for the advice i will implement it , about QuantConnect do you advise to have the paid subscription + also data from polygon or the data are enough from QC?

replies.author: ryank001
replies.body:
Honestly for just backtesting stocks, QC's built-in data is plenty — you don't need Polygon on top. Their US equity data already handles survivorship bias (includes delisted names), which is the main thing you're paying for elsewhere. Start there.

The paid sub mostly buys you more compute, faster backtests, and live-trading nodes — not better data. So I'd only jump to it once you're actually running things enough that the free tier's queue times annoy you, or you're ready to go live.

Polygon really only makes sense if you leave QC and build your own local stack, or you need something QC doesn't cover (tick data, specific coverage). For where you're at, QC's own data alone gets the job done.

comments.author: hikewithcaramel
comments.body: Backtesting is great but it doesn't account for slippage, broker fees, latency. If you forward test with a sufficient and clean data set and find the same edge as one of your backrests then that's the golden goose
